facts.query: How many times would you have to fold a sheet of paper to reach the Moon?
facts.explanation: Every fold doubles the thickness of the stack, and doubling grows astonishingly fast. A sheet starts thinner than a fingernail, yet after a few dozen imaginary folds it would stretch past the Moon. In practice nobody can fold real paper more than a handful of times.

facts.query: How does a nuclear power plant make electricity?
facts.topic: How a nuclear power plant works
facts.explanation: A nuclear power plant is a steam engine with an unusual heat source. Splitting uranium atoms releases heat, which turns water into steam, and the steam spins a turbine connected to a generator. The water is then cooled and reused in a closed loop.

facts.label: Split uranium atoms
facts.sourceNote: US DOE Office of Nuclear Energy, nuclear fission basics
facts.title: Split uranium atoms
facts.description: Neutrons strike uranium-235 nuclei in the fuel rods. Each nucleus splits, releasing heat and more neutrons that split further nuclei.

facts.label: Control the chain reaction
facts.sourceNote: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, pressurized-water reactor overview
facts.title: Control the chain reaction
facts.description: Control rods that absorb neutrons are raised or lowered so the chain reaction stays steady instead of speeding up.

facts.label: Heat the water
facts.sourceNote: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, pressurized-water reactor overview
facts.title: Heat the water
facts.description: Water pumped through the reactor core absorbs the heat. It is kept under high pressure so it stays liquid.

facts.label: Make steam
facts.sourceNote: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, pressurized-water reactor overview
facts.title: Make steam
facts.description: In the steam generator, the hot pressurized water boils water in a separate loop into high-pressure steam.

facts.label: Spin the turbine
facts.sourceNote: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, pressurized-water reactor overview
facts.title: Spin the turbine
facts.description: The steam rushes through a turbine and spins its blades.

facts.label: Generate electricity
facts.sourceNote: US Energy Information Administration, how electricity is generated
facts.title: Generate electricity
facts.description: The turbine turns a generator, where spinning magnets and coils produce electric current for the grid.

facts.label: Cool and recycle
facts.sourceNote: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, pressurized-water reactor overview
facts.title: Cool and recycle
facts.description: A condenser cools the spent steam back into water using water from a river, sea or cooling tower, and the water returns to the steam generator.

facts.query: How much heavier is a proton than an electron?
facts.explanation: Protons and electrons carry equal and opposite electric charges, but they are wildly different in mass. It takes well over a thousand electrons to match one proton, which is why almost all of an atom's mass sits in its tiny nucleus.

facts.query: What is the air we breathe made of?
facts.explanation: Air is mostly nitrogen, with oxygen making up most of the rest. Argon, an unreactive noble gas, is a distant third. Carbon dioxide is only a trace gas, yet it traps enough heat to shape Earth's climate.

facts.query: How fast does sound travel through different materials?
facts.topic: Speed of sound in different materials
facts.explanation: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, so it travels at different speeds through different materials. It is slowest in gases like air, several times faster in water, and fastest in stiff solids such as iron and aluminium.

facts.query: How deep are the layers inside the Earth?
facts.explanation: Earth is layered like an onion. A thin rocky crust floats on a thick mantle of hot rock that flows very slowly, and below that lies an iron core: a liquid outer core whose churning makes Earth's magnetic field, and a solid inner core at the centre.

facts.query: What are the greatest discoveries in physics?
facts.explanation: Modern physics grew from Newton's laws of motion and gravity. Electricity, magnetism and light were unified next, then discoveries inside the atom and the theories of relativity and quantum mechanics transformed our picture of nature. Giant experiments have since confirmed predictions made decades earlier.
